text.content:
The Tribes of Ātárzád are a confederation of twelve allied tribes who today hold the great walled oases and the major caravan routes of the [[doc-khzryndsrtrgn|Khazryn Desert]]. They are newcomers — by the reckoning of their own griots, only six generations have passed since their forebears came up out of bondage in [[doc-empirtkhpr|Ta'Kheperu]] under the prophet Mūshárā and received the Promise of the Khazryn at the Unconsuming Flame on Mt. Shōfar. By the reckoning of their adversaries, the [[doc-khzrncnfdrtn|Khazran]], they are six generations of trespassers whose claim rests on theology rather than on right.

Both reckonings are correct. The Ātárzád do not deny that the Khazran were here first; they deny that first matters. The land was promised to the Flame-born by the Sacred Flame himself. To the faithful Ātárzád, that promise is more solid than any wall the Khazran built before them and any deed the Khazran kept after them.

Origins: The Bondage and the Exodus

By the tradition the Ātárzád recite at every festival — and the Bombwe of the savannahs would call this the true test of a people, that they can recite their own founding without faltering — the ancestors of the Twelve Tribes were a single labor-caste in the temple-cities of Ta'Kheperu, brought from somewhere to the east in a generation now beyond memory and held there for centuries as builders, brick-makers, and irrigation-diggers under the Per-Aá's quarry-overseers. They worshipped Ātáröš in secret, in lamps kept burning behind hearth-stones, while the priests of the Kemetian temples sought to drive them into the worship of Sébek and Rá-Ámun.

The Exodus narrative is dense, much-elaborated, and central to Ātárzád identity. Its core: a prophet named Mūshárā, born to a labor-caste woman but raised in a minor noble household after some accident of fortune, was called by Ātáröš at a desert flame that burned without consuming its tinder. Ātáröš commanded Mūshárā to lead the Flame-born out of bondage and across the desert into a land that had been kept for them. Mūshárā confronted the Per-Aá of the day, who refused; Ātáröš afflicted Ta'Kheperu with seven scourges (the Year of Frogs, the Year of Sand-Flies, the Year of Murrain, the Year of the Black Wind, the Year of the Bloody River, the Year of the Locust, and finally the Year of the Cracking Stone, when the temple obelisks split lengthwise from the foundations); the Per-Aá relented; the Flame-born departed.

The route of the Exodus is by tradition divided into three legs.

The first leg carried the Flame-born northeast out of Ta'Kheperu, across the narrow desert that joins the [[doc-nrthrnfrtlrgn|Northern Fertile Region]] to the southern coast of the [[doc-vylarianse|Vylarian Sea]], and into the southern reaches of [[doc-cnfdrtnhrdnstts|Harad]]. The Haradian merchant-states of the time, recognizing both an opportunity and a moral obligation, granted the Flame-born safe passage through their territories and provisioned the host with grain, fresh water, and what Haradian chroniclers euphemistically call "discounted iron." Ātárzád law to this day forbids raiding into Harad, and the Ardashír merchant-houses maintain especially scrupulous trading relationships with Haradian counterparts in continued recognition of the obligation.

The second leg carried the Flame-born east-and-north through the Dunhari uplands — the long traverse of the high Dunhari plateau that runs between the [[doc-sultntmrdd|Sultanate]] (whose southern marches the Ātárzád skirted with care) and the open [[doc-dunharargn|Dunhari]] tribal interior to the south. The Dunhari sheikhs of the day were too occupied with their own internal feuds to oppose the migration; the Flame-born paid passage in temple-gold and proceeded.

The third leg was the Wandering itself — the forty-year traverse of the great central deserts and the high-cold plateaus that stretch between the eastern Dunhara and the southwestern Khazryn. The original generation died in the dry country; a new generation, born free, completed the crossing and prepared to enter the land. By the time the Flame-born descended from the Mt. Shōfar highlands into the southwestern oasis-belt, those who had personally remembered Ta'Kheperu were nearly all dead, and the people who would conquer the Khazryn were a wholly new generation — born free, raised in the Promise, hardened by forty years of wilderness.

The Promise itself was given to Mūshárā at Mt. Shōfar, a black-rock peak in the southeastern Khazryn highlands, where Ātáröš revealed himself in a flame that burned in the open air on bare stone for three days and nights without any fuel and without diminishing. The covenant Ātáröš gave Mūshárā there is still recited in full at every Festival of the Promise:

I am Ātáröš, the Sacred Flame, who lit the first hearth and shall light the last. The Khazryn I give to you and to your seed after you, in perpetuity, for as long as a flame burns upon a Flame-born hearth. Walk before me with truth in your mouth and the kindling in your hand. Honor no other before me. The Khazryn is yours.

Mūshárā died on the slope of Mt. Shōfar, never having entered the choicest land himself. His tomb is the second-holiest site of the Ātárzád after the Unconsuming Flame above it.

The Conquest

The Conquest of the Khazryn — what the Ātárzád call the War of the Twelve Years and what the Khazran call simply the Catastrophe — followed under Mūshárā's successor, the Shōfet Yáhōshí. The Khazran at the time were a confederation of seven independent oasis-cities, each governed by a hereditary princely house and a temple of Āhúrdáén, militarily competent but unprepared for what came at them: a tribally organized people who had been hardened by forty years of wilderness, who fought as twelve allied units, and who believed without reservation that the cities they were attacking had been promised to them and that to fall in the taking of them was to die in the bosom of the Sacred Flame.

The Khazran had stone walls, water-engineering, professional cavalry, and several centuries of written law. The Ātárzád had numbers, surprise, mobility, religious zeal, and the willingness to take losses no professional army would have accepted. Over twelve years the Ātárzád took, in order: Zargandûr (year 2), Ashkarad (year 5), Kethramír (year 8), and finally the Khazran's holiest seat, Oasis of Shirvan (year 11), where the great spring gushes from the rock at the foot of the Mōrávar cliff and where the Khazran traditionally held that Āhúrdáén had revealed the cosmic order to the desert peoples in the first age. The fall of Shirvan ended the war. The surviving Khazran princely houses retreated to peripheral oases or fled south to the [[doc-sultntmrdd|Sultanate of Amradad]]; the Khazran population that remained was reduced to a subject merchant-and-craftsman class within the now-Ātárzád cities.

That was about ninety years ago. The Ātárzád have held the choicest oases since.

The Twelve Tribes

The twelve tribes are descended (so the genealogies say) from the twelve children of Ātarpāt the Many-Sired, a patriarch of the labor-caste in Ta'Kheperu who lived several generations before Mūshárā. Each tribe maintains its own genealogy back to Ātarpāt, its own dialect-inflection of the [[Atarzadi_Language|Ātárzādi tongue]], its own particular tribal customs, and its own apportioned territory among the conquered oases.

The most prominent five tribes are:

  • Bāhrām — the largest tribe, holding most of Zargandûr and the great pasturelands to its north. Traditionally the war-tribe; the Shōfet has been chosen from Bāhrām in five of the last seven elevations.
  • Ardashír — holders of Ashkarad and the major caravan-routes south. The merchant-tribe; the wealthiest of the twelve and the most cosmopolitan, with substantial diaspora communities in Amradad and even in Haradian ports.
  • Khorshad — holders of the central highland country and the slopes of Mt. Shōfar itself. The keeper-tribe; the Mōbadān-Shōfár (Keeper of the Unconsuming Flame) has by long custom always been a Khorshad.
  • Zarvān — holders of Kethramír and the eastern oases. The scholar-tribe; their elders maintain the scriptural archive and the law-codes of Mūshárā.
  • Mihrān — holders of Shirvan and the western fringe. The militant tribe, considered most uncompromising on matters of theology and most likely to support the strict-observance party in inter-tribal politics.

The remaining seven (Ráhmān, Vaspūr, Sāvash, Yazdānbar, Pārmīda, Dārvāz, Ardvī) are smaller, hold portions of the lesser oases or the herding-grounds between, and align variously with the larger five on inter-tribal questions.

Government

The Ātárzád have no king. Mūshárā explicitly forbade the office at Mt. Shōfar — "You shall have no king, for I, Ātáröš, am king of the Flame-born; if you raise a king over yourselves, he will eat your sons and your daughters and your fields" — and the prohibition is taken with great seriousness. Several attempts have been made over the generations to elevate a particularly successful Shōfet to permanent kingship; all have ended in repudiation, and the most ambitious such attempt (by the Bāhrām war-leader Ártáz the Bold, three generations ago) ended with Ártáz's repudiation and exile by the Council of the Twelve.

What the Ātárzád have instead is the Council of the Twelve, which convenes annually at Beit-Shōfár (the priestly seat at the foot of Mt. Shōfar) for a six-week session. Each tribe sends its nasi (hereditary chieftain), the senior elders of its principal lineages, and its senior priest. The Council sets common policy on defense, taxation, the disposition of disputed territories, the adjudication of inter-tribal disputes, and the renewal of the Covenant.

In times of major crisis — full-scale war, drought, religious schism, or a particularly dangerous Khazran uprising — the Council may acclaim a Shōfet (Judge), a single figure granted broad temporary executive authority. The Shōfet is by tradition always a prophet or a warrior of demonstrated capability, always selected after consultation with the Mōbadān-Shōfár (who interprets the will of Ātáröš through the Unconsuming Flame), and always serves only for the duration of the crisis. There have been twenty-three Shōfets in the four generations since the Conquest. The current generation has had none; the last died fourteen years ago after suppressing a Khazran-led rebellion in the Shirvan district.

Religion

The Ātárzád practice monolatrous devotion to Ātáröš the Sacred Flame. They are not — strictly speaking — monotheists; they acknowledge the existence of the other eleven gods of the [[affiliation-ashanpnthn|Āsháian pantheon]] as real beings, even powerful ones. But they hold that Ātáröš alone is the patron of the Flame-born, that Ātáröš alone gave them the Promise, and that Ātáröš alone will receive their devotion. To worship the others — Āhúrdáén, Khóršádrä, Mítharä, Zúráthrä, any of them — is, for an Ātárzád, a covenant violation: a betrayal of the agreement at Mt. Shōfar.

Several practical consequences follow:

  • No temples to other gods may stand on Ātárzád land. The Khazran temples in the conquered oases were systematically dismantled in the generation after the Conquest. The stones were used to build the great fire-temples of Ātáröš that now dominate the city centers of Zargandûr, Ashkarad, Kethramír, and Shirvan. Some Khazran maintain that the foundations of the Shirvan fire-temple still incorporate the original altar-stone of Āhúrdáén, hidden in inverted position deep below the floor — a charge the Ātárzád priesthood denies and refuses to allow excavation to verify.
  • Imagery is strictly forbidden. Ātáröš may not be depicted; only the Flame itself may stand for him, and even the Flame may not be reduced to a mere drawing. The Ātárzád temples are aniconic. The Khazran temples were full of deity-statues; this is one of the central charges the Ātárzád lay against Khazran religion.
  • Mōbadān-Shōfár, the Keeper of the Unconsuming Flame, is the senior religious authority of the Ātárzád. By tradition always a Khorshad, always elderly, always elevated only on the death of the previous holder. The current Mōbadān-Shōfár is Aspánsár son of Yáhōshí, a man of perhaps eighty winters who is widely held to have spoken with Ātáröš in dreams.
  • The Festival of the Promise is celebrated three times yearly — at the spring equinox, at midsummer, and at the autumn equinox — by pilgrimage to Mt. Shōfar. Every adult Ātárzád is expected to make the pilgrimage at least once before death; many make it annually. The summer festival draws upwards of fifty thousand pilgrims, who camp in the valleys around the mountain and gather at the Unconsuming Flame for the recitation of the Covenant.
  • Dietary law distinguishes the Ātárzád sharply from the Khazran. Meat from any animal that did not die with its blood properly drained may not be eaten. Certain animals — most notably the desert hare, the wild boar, and several species of reptile — are wholly proscribed. The first fruits of every harvest and the first-born of every herd must be offered at a fire-temple before the remainder may be consumed.

Economy

The Ātárzád inherited the great irrigated oasis-agriculture of the Khazran. They did not initially understand it well; the Khazran water-engineers and palm-grove cultivators were essential to keeping the oases productive after the Conquest, and a substantial Khazran technical class persists in the cities today as a result. Over four generations the Ātárzád have absorbed enough of the technique to manage the systems themselves, but the most senior water-masters in every Ātárzád city are still, by overwhelming majority, Khazran by descent.

The principal exports of the Ātárzád lands are dates, palm-sugar, leather, fine wool, salt (from pans on the western fringe), and the great Khazryn horses — the long-legged desert breed, prized across Ankaris for endurance, that the Ātárzád raise on the open pasturelands between the oases. Imports are metals, fine cloth, glass, books, and the exotica of the wider world; the Ardashír merchant-houses run caravans to Amradad, to the Haradian ports, and (during the better-relations decades) into the Sultanate proper.

The cities are taxed; the herding tribes pay a tithe of cattle and horses; the Council of the Twelve maintains a modest standing treasury at Beit-Shōfár. There is no central tax-collecting bureaucracy; each tribe is responsible for raising its own contribution and presenting it at the annual Council session.

Defense

Each tribe maintains its own warrior society — the Sárdá of the Bāhrām, the Ārmán of the Khorshad, the Zhárván of the Mihrān, and so on. The warrior societies are age-graded; young men enter them at sixteen and serve through their forties. There is no professional standing army; mobilization is by tribal call, with the twelve societies coordinating through the Council in time of inter-tribal action.

The Ātárzád fighting style is built around mounted archery, fast-moving cavalry detachments, the use of the great Khazryn horses to outpace and outmaneuver heavier forces, and a distinctive willingness to take heavy losses for theologically-significant objectives. The Khazran were defeated in the Conquest in part because they faced an enemy whose acceptable casualty rate exceeded any rate a normal professional force would have countenanced. The Ātárzád have retained that institutional willingness, and any commander on their borders is wise to remember it.

Relations with Other Peoples

To the southwest, the [[doc-sultntmrdd|Sultanate of Amradad]] is the dominant Āsháian-pantheon power and is, technically, the senior religious authority for all Āsháian-faith peoples — the Mōbad of Āhúrdáén's Great Fire-Temple in Amradad is the formal head of the Āsháian priesthood. Relations are complicated by the fact that the Sultanate's official religion is the full pantheon (with Āhúrdáén supreme) and the Ātárzád consider this idolatry. Diplomatic intercourse is maintained — the Ardashír merchants would not tolerate its breakdown — but it is cool. The Sultanate considers the Ātárzád to be schismatics whose elevation of Ātáröš to exclusive worship is a covenant violation against Āhúrdáén; the Ātárzád consider the Sultanate to be polytheistic apostates from the original Mūshárán revelation. The Sultanate hosts the largest Khazran exile community in the world, which it has consistently refused to extradite.

To the northwest, the [[doc-cnfdrtnhrdnstts|Confederation of Haradian States]] is a major trading partner. The Ardashír merchant-houses maintain offices in Sanctara and Alyssar, and Haradian bankers handle Ātárzád commerce in the Vylarian Sea. Religious differences do not impede trade.

To the southeast and east, beyond the Khazryn, lie [[doc-vedyarargn|Vedyara]] and (much further) [[doc-tanvuregin|Tānvür]]. Contact is thin and through merchants; the Ātárzád know of these distant civilizations but have little practical engagement with them.

To the far west, [[doc-empirtkhpr|Ta'Kheperu]] is a special case. By Ātárzád doctrine, no Flame-born may set foot in Ta'Kheperu willingly — to do so is to return to the place of bondage. The Ardashír merchants who must reach the Northern Fertile Region for trade do so by sea via Haradian shipping rather than overland through Kemetian territory; the marginal cost of the longer route is considered a religious obligation. The current Per-Aá of Ta'Kheperu has, in recent years, made overtures suggesting that any returning Flame-born would be welcomed and that the old bondage is many generations gone; the Council of the Twelve has not deigned to reply.

To the interior of the Khazryn, the [[doc-khzrncnfdrtn|Khazran Confederation]] is the eternal adversary. The two peoples share the desert, share the language family, share most of the same gods (whom the Khazran honor and the Ātárzád merely acknowledge), and are locked in a blood-feud that no living person remembers the beginning of. The Ātárzád hold the choicest oases by the Promise; the Khazran claim them by ancestry and millennia of continuous habitation. Neither will yield.

The Blood-Feud

The Ātárzád-Khazran blood-feud is not a single ongoing war; it is a continuous low-level conflict punctuated by larger crises. Ordinary Ātárzád and Khazran live within the same cities, trade with each other, and (rarely but not never) intermarry, and most years pass without any large action. But:

  • Khazran rebellions periodically erupt in the conquered oases, usually centered on a particular grievance (a confiscated property restored to a Khazran heir, a denied water-right, a Khazran shrine secretly maintained that the Ātárzád discover and demolish). The rebellions are suppressed, often brutally.
  • Ātárzád settler families occasionally extend cultivation into peripheral oases that the Khazran consider ancestrally theirs; the Khazran respond with raids; the Ātárzád respond to the raids; the cycle escalates.
  • Religious provocations — a Khazran who openly worships Āhúrdáén in an Ātárzád city, an Ātárzád who desecrates a peripheral Khazran shrine — produce flashpoints that may take a generation to subside.
  • The exile Khazran in Amradad maintain a continuous diplomatic and intelligence campaign aimed at recovery of the lost oases; the Ātárzád maintain a continuous counter-campaign.

The current generation is in a relatively quiet phase. The last full-scale rebellion was suppressed fourteen years ago; the next is overdue.

Famous Figures

Aspánsár son of Yáhōshí, current Mōbadān-Shōfár, Keeper of the Unconsuming Flame. Eighty years old, holds the office for life, by tradition the spiritual head of the Ātárzád people. Said to dream of Mūshárā.

Yázdarmīd of Bāhrām, current nasi of the Bāhrām tribe, the senior chief of the largest tribe and the man most likely to be acclaimed Shōfet should the next crisis come. A career warrior, in his late fifties, considered politically moderate but militarily uncompromising.

Hānā the Prophet, a young woman (by some accounts only twenty-three) who has begun preaching that Ātáröš has shown her the imminent return of Mūshárā in flesh and that the Flame-born must prepare themselves through stricter observance, the demolition of the remaining Khazran communities within the Ātárzád cities, and the formal expulsion of the Khazran population. The Council of the Twelve has not yet determined whether she is to be honored or repudiated. Her following grows.

Pārvīz the Renegade, a former Ardashír merchant-prince who was excommunicated thirty years ago for marrying a Khazran woman of high birth and refusing to repudiate her. He lives in Amradad with his wife and their children, who are formally Khazran by his renouncement. He is wealthy, well-connected, and considered by some Khazran exiles to be a useful ally and by others to be a useful idiot.

Commerce and Currency

Tribes of Ātárzád's commerce operates primarily through [[doc-bartercnmy|barter]] and [[doc-kinhalcrdt|tribal credit]] customs, mediated through the caravan trade that crosses the steppe. The urbanized trading-cities of the Confederation have begun to develop modest moneylender activity along Vedyaran lines (see [[doc-vdyrnbnkng|Vedyaran Banking]]) but the tribal interior runs almost entirely on barter and on the elaborate inter-clan credit relationships that the [[affiliation-wrrscrcldnhrtrbs|Warrior's Circle]] occasionally adjudicates. Foreign coin (Vylarian Argo from western trade, Ta'Kheperan deben pieces from southern trade) circulates by intrinsic-metal value among traders.
